text: Claes Moeyaert followed Rembrandt in his use of red chalk. He was born in Durgerdam, and as a young man he is thought to have traveled to Italy to see its art. At 25 he married Grietje Claes, and he was possibly in business with Pieter Lastman in Amsterdam. He painted many biblical and mythological scenes, and he also designed the triumphal arch that Amsterdam built for the arrival of Maria de Medici. He had three children. Two of them needed care, and he looked after them in his own home.

Karl Hofer lost his father four weeks after he was born in Karlsruhe, and as a boy he went to live in an orphanage. At 14 he began a bookshop apprenticeship. He later studied painting under Hans Thoma, and a Swiss patron named Theodor Reinhart paid him a regular sum in return for several paintings each year. Hofer lived in Paris for five years, where Cézanne and the early Picasso influenced him. He never joined Die Brücke. The Nazis counted his work as degenerate art, and he also served as director of the Berlin Academy of Fine Arts.

Ambrosius Benson came from Italy but trained in Bruges under Gerard David. He became a citizen of the city, was made a master in 1519, and later served the painters' guild as dean and governor. His workshop was large, and his pictures sold abroad, especially in Spain. That is why many of his best works hang in Spanish museums and churches. He painted the Magdalen reading many times, and one version is in the National Gallery in London. He died in Flanders in 1550.

David Vinckboons had at least ten children. One son became a cartographer and two others became architects. He was born in Mechelen, and the family moved to Antwerp around 1580 and then to Middelburg after the Spanish occupation of Antwerp in 1585. Karel van Mander wrote that his only teacher was his father, who painted on canvas with watercolours. Vinckboons painted elegant figures in park landscapes, village festivals and Bible scenes, and he took on pupils such as Claes Janszoon Visscher. He died in Amsterdam.

Michiel van Musscher had so many teachers that he kept a record of them. They included Martinus Saeghmolen, Abraham van den Tempel, Gabriel Metsu and Adriaen van Ostade. Houbraken was amazed that he became so skilled with so few hours of study, and he put it down to natural talent. Musscher was born in Rotterdam and moved to Amsterdam, where Jonas Witsen introduced him to his friends as a portrait painter. In 1698 he painted Alexander Menshikov and François Lefort while Peter the Great's Grand Embassy was in Holland. He died in 1705.

François Clouet inherited his father's nickname, Janet. He was born in Tours and learned painting from his father, Jean Clouet. Like his father he became groom of the chamber and painter in ordinary to the king, and a document from December 1541 shows the king handing him his father's estate. He made death masks of Francis I and Henry II, and he painted the decorations and banners for their funerals. Few of the works credited to him are backed by documents.

Julius Caesar Ibbetson got his odd middle name because his mother fell on the ice and went into early labour, so he was delivered by caesarean section. He tried to hide the name all his life. He was apprenticed to a ship painter in Hull and then spent about ten years in London restoring pictures. In 1787 he went to Peking as draughtsman on the first British embassy there, and he drew the animals and plants on the journey. Later he settled in Ambleside and became friends with Wordsworth and Coleridge.

John Leech was drawing at three, when the sculptor John Flaxman found him sketching on his mother's knee. He went to Charterhouse School, where William Makepeace Thackeray was a fellow pupil and a lifelong friend. At sixteen he began to study medicine at St Bartholomew's Hospital, and his anatomical drawings earned praise. His first designs were published when he was eighteen. He later drew political satire and social comedy for Punch, and he made four plates for the first edition of Charles Dickens's A Christmas Carol in 1843.

Albert König grew up in very poor conditions, the son of a village blacksmith in Eschede. As a boy he worked as a herd boy in the nearby village of Endeholz besides going to school. He then trained for three years under the decorative painter Albert Oehm, and later he studied at the arts and crafts school in Düsseldorf. In 1927 he moved into a new house with a studio in Unterlüß. There he lived in seclusion and worked on woodcuts and paintings. He treated his studio almost like a sacred room.

Claude Augustin Duflos came from an old middle class family that originally lived in Picardy. His father, Claude Duflos, was engraver to the king in Paris. Duflos worked as an architect and a printmaker, and he was born in Paris in 1700. He had several collections of prints published at the shop of his nephew Pierre Duflos le Jeune, and he made many engravings after the work of François Boucher. Scholars also credit him with erotic illustrations for an edition of Voltaire's La Pucelle d'Orléans, based on drawings by Clément-Pierre Marillier. He died in Paris in 1786.

Abraham van Diepenbeeck designed glass windows for churches and monasteries in Antwerp. He was born in 's-Hertogenbosch, where his father was a glass painter, and he left for Antwerp after his father died in 1620. Around 1632 Rubens asked him to go to France and draw frescoes by Primaticcio and Nicolò dell'Abate in Paris and Fontainebleau. He also helped the workshop of Rubens with cartoons for woven wall hangings. He had trouble with the guild all his career. When he was made dean against his own wishes, he refused to hand in its accounts.

Adolf Schrödter's father was a copper engraver in Schwedt. The son studied engraving in Berlin, and by 1827 he had decided to paint instead. A year later he went to Düsseldorf to work with Wilhelm von Schadow. Botany was his hobby. He drew cartoons and wrote satires for a new humor magazine, and in 1859 he moved to Karlsruhe, where he taught ornamentation at the new art school until 1872. He worked in painting, etching, woodcut and lithography.

A street and a school in Haslach carry the name of Carl Sandhaas. He was the illegitimate son of Maria Margarete Sandhaas, and the painter Johann Baptist Seele may have been his father. He grew up in Haslach and moved to his uncle, a theatre painter, in Darmstadt at 15. He later studied history painting in Munich. After a spell in Frankfurt as an illustrator for a publisher, he lived in Haslach from 1830 until his death, with a few breaks along the way. He painted landscapes and portraits, and he also illustrated literary and mythological works.

Cham, whose real name was Charles Amédée de Noé, drew about 40,000 pictures in his career. His family wanted him to go to a polytechnic school, but he took painting classes with Nicolas Charlet and Paul Delaroche instead. His first book, Monsieur Lajaunisse, came out in 1839, and four years later he began to publish in Le Charivari, where he stayed on the staff for 30 years. Later works included Proudhon en voyage. Near the end of his life he wrote a number of comic plays. He died in Paris in 1879.

Bernhard Vogel learned the mezzotint technique from his teachers Christoph Weigel and Elias Christoph Heiß, and he later married the daughter of Heiß. He made a series of portraits, among them ones of his father and his teachers. His main work is a collection of mezzotints showing the painter Johann Kupetzky and his pictures, which Vogel carried on at his own cost. He was born in Nuremberg in 1683 and died there in 1737. His son Johann Christoph Vogel also became an engraver.

Will Hicok Low entered the Paris atelier of Jean-Léon Gérôme in 1873 and later joined the classes of Carolus-Duran. He stayed in Barbizon and Montigny-sur-Loing. Low painted panels and medallions for the Waldorf-Astoria Hotel in New York, and he also made stained glass windows for churches. He was a close friend of R. L. Stevenson and wrote a book of reminiscences called A Chronicle of Friendships. A series of murals in the New York State Education Department rotunda in Albany is his work. His design was used on the one-dollar silver certificate History Instructing Youth.

Johann Salver engraved a series of portraits of the bishops of Würzburg, all the way back to the early days of the diocese. He came from Forchheim and worked in Würzburg as engraver to the court and the university. The coats of arms he gave the early bishops come more from the ideas of his own century than from history. For a doctoral thesis printed in 1723 he engraved a view of the city that Balthasar Neumann had sketched. His third marriage produced a son, Johann Octavian Salver, who became a genealogist. Salver died in 1738.
